title: A bruised reed (Matthew 12:1–21)
hookLine: a cracked screen, a smoking wick: he won't break the bruised reed
tomorrow: can a friend ever be more family than family?

cards: A phone with a spiderweb crack across the screen still works, if you're careful. Press too hard and the glass gives.
Or blow out a candle and catch the smell: that thin gray ribbon of smoke, the wick still glowing orange at the tip. One breath would finish it. One breath could also bring it back.
Matthew has a picture for exactly that moment, a reed already cracked, a wick already smoking. And he sets it in the middle of a fight.

teach.b: The fight is about the sabbath. Hungry disciples pick grain as they walk on the day of rest, and some Pharisees object.
Jesus answers from scripture, with a line heard here before: "if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless."

Then, in a synagogue, a man with a withered hand. Jesus heals him and says: "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days." It's an argument about how to honor the sabbath, not whether to, with scripture on every side.
The argument turns sharp, and Jesus withdraws.
Right there, Matthew quotes Isaiah about God's chosen servant: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory."
A bruised reed is bent and cracked; one more push and it snaps. Smoking flax is a lamp wick nearly out, more smoke than flame. Both are one touch from finished.
This servant doesn't finish them. He leaves the cracked reed standing and lets the wick keep its glow.
And notice where Matthew puts the picture: right after a withered hand is made whole.

teach.h: HE WON'T BREAK THE BRUISED REED.
teach.b: In the middle of a quarrel, he points at gentleness.

how: Some Christians read Matthew 12:20 when caring for people who are grieving, sick or worn out, and some hospital chaplains and pastoral carers point to the bruised reed as a picture of their work.

s: the sabbath arguments were about whether to keep the sabbath at all
they were about how to honor it: "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days."
a bruised reed in this picture is already snapped in two
it's cracked but still standing; the servant won't break it.
Matthew quotes Isaiah right after the sabbath healing
he quotes Isaiah's servant: a bruised reed shall he not break.

games.q: your little brother's science project collapses the night before it's due. he's half crying, half furious. what's the bruised-reed move?
o: explain what went wrong, so he learns it for next time.
tell him it's no big deal, it's only a project.
steady the pieces with him, and save the lesson for later.
games.why: the servant in Isaiah, as Matthew quotes him, won't break a bruised reed or quench smoking flax. cracked moments call for steady hands first.

practice: Find something fragile within reach: a leaf, a dried flower, an egg, a paper cup. Hold it in your open palm and feel how little pressure it would take to crush it, and how little it takes to keep it whole.
Rest your attention there while you breathe, and let one fragile person come to mind.

wordCard.voice: A bruised reed. Cracked but still standing, in Isaiah's picture that Matthew borrows: the servant won't snap it.

orig.note: Greek: a reed, a cane. Matthew 12:20: a bruised reed shall he not break.

carryVoice: Your line: the bruised reed. Cracked is not the same thing as finished. Until tomorrow.
